title: Infosys, Truist Expand Hyderabad AI Centre, Onboard Over 1,000
excerpt: Infosys will build, operate and transfer Truist's AI-first Global Capability Center in Hyderabad, consolidating the US bank's multiple India suppliers into one model as more than 1,000 colleagues join this month.
body:
• Infosys and Truist are expanding their collaboration to build out Truist's AI-first Global Capability Center in Hyderabad, consolidating work now spread across multiple suppliers in India into one integrated operating model.
  • More than 1,000 colleagues have been onboarded into the centre and will be celebrated later in October 2026 — the centre is already operating at scale, not a plan on paper.
  • Infosys will build, scale and then transition the centre into a self-sustaining centre of excellence using its Build, Operate and Transfer model and Infosys Topaz AI suite.
  • For Indian tech professionals: the roles sit across AI, technology, data and operations for a top-10 US bank with $556 billion in assets — Hyderabad, not a US relocation, is the hiring centre for this expansion.

Infosys is expanding its collaboration with Truist, one of the largest financial services companies in the United States, to support the continued build-out of the bank's AI-first Global Capability Center (GCC) in Hyderabad, the companies announced on October 19 in Bengaluru. The centre will onboard more than 1,000 colleagues this month, a milestone the two companies said they will celebrate later in October.

The expansion consolidates capabilities that Truist currently receives through multiple supplier relationships in India into a more unified, integrated operating model run with Infosys. In the joint announcement distributed by PR Newswire, the companies said Infosys will use its financial services expertise and AI-first capabilities to accelerate transformation and drive enterprise-wide value creation for the bank.

A Build, Operate and Transfer Centre

The model matters more than the headcount. Infosys will help Truist build, scale and transition a self-sustaining centre of excellence that integrates AI, technology, data and operations into a single delivery framework. The stated aims are to reduce third-party dependency, manage global delivery complexity and cultivate future-ready technology talent in India.

https://x.com/Infosys/status/2112136814865547684

Dennis Gada, executive vice president and global head of banking and financial services at Infosys, tied the work directly to that model and to Infosys Topaz, the company's AI suite.

"By leveraging Infosys Topaz, our proven Build, Operate and Transfer enablement model and deep financial services expertise, we are committed to helping Truist build a resilient, scalable digital core — and unlock AI value at scale — with trust and governance built in."

— Dennis Gada, EVP and Global Head of Banking and Financial Services, Infosys

That structure — build and operate first, transfer later — is how large US banks have increasingly set up India centres in recent years: a services partner absorbs the hiring, transition and compliance load, then hands over a functioning centre rather than a collection of vendor contracts.

Why Truist Is Building in Hyderabad

Truist described the GCC as a strategic investment, not a cost-cutting back office. India already hosts a base of Truist contract professionals working across engineering, data and operations, according to the announcement, and the Hyderabad centre is meant to deepen that base into a hub that can move faster on digital and AI work.

"Our Global Capability Center in India is a strategic investment in Truist's future. As we accelerate our transformation into a more agile, AI-enabled enterprise, we are intentionally building global capabilities that allow us to move faster, innovate at scale, and better serve our clients."

— Steve Hagerman, Chief Information Officer, Truist

Truist Financial Corporation is headquartered in Charlotte, North Carolina, and is a top-10 US commercial bank, with total assets of $556 billion as of June 30, 2026. For a bank of that scale, consolidating India delivery under one partner simplifies governance — fewer suppliers to audit and one operating model for data and AI work.

What It Signals for India's GCC Economy

The deal fits a broader pattern: global banks no longer treat India centres as overflow capacity. The announcement frames Hyderabad as a hub for innovation and digital capability, centred on AI-led work — scaling strategic capabilities and improving client experience — rather than routine processing.

For Infosys, the win deepens a long-standing banking relationship at a moment when large financial clients are moving from modernising legacy systems to deploying AI across functions. Independent coverage made the same point for investors: a BOT engagement at this scale shows an ability to win strategic operating-model work, though it carries transition risk as staff and work migrate from multiple suppliers into one framework.

What to Watch Next

Neither company disclosed a contract value or duration, so the financial impact will only become visible in later commentary. The near-term markers are operational: whether the late-October onboarding celebration proceeds as planned, whether the centre continues to scale beyond the first 1,000 colleagues, and whether Infosys cites the Truist model as a template for other large banking clients consolidating their India presence. For Hyderabad's technology workforce, the immediate fact is simpler — a top-10 US bank is building its AI centre there, and it has already staffed it at four-figure scale.
